section.title: The Second Journey: Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens
section.sectionRationale: In three cities the gospel meets three responses. At Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures that the Christ must suffer and rise, and a mob accuses the believers of proclaiming another king, Jesus. At Berea the hearers eagerly test his message against Scripture. At Athens Paul confronts the sophisticated pagan mind head on, standing at the Areopagus to proclaim the one Creator God who commands all to repent because He has fixed a day of judgment and raised the Man who will judge.
section.thesis: The risen Christ is the crucified Messiah promised in Scripture and the Lord of every nation, so that the gospel both fulfils the Hebrew Scriptures for the synagogue and dismantles idolatry for the philosopher, summoning Jew and Greek alike to repent in light of the coming judgment guaranteed by the resurrection.
section.frameNote: Three cities: the reasoned proclamation and uproar at Thessalonica; the noble, Scripture-testing Bereans; and Athens, where Paul is provoked by the idols, debates the philosophers, and delivers the Areopagus address on the unknown God, ending with repentance, judgment, and resurrection.

verses.text: When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ,” he declared.
Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women.

The Jews, however, became jealous. So they brought in some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and sent the city into an uproar. They raided Jason’s house in search of Paul and Silas, hoping to bring them out to the people.
But when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other brothers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here,
and Jason has welcomed them into his home. They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus!”
On hearing this, the crowd and city officials were greatly disturbed.
And they collected bond from Jason and the others and then released them.
As soon as night had fallen, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. On arriving there, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true.
As a result, many of them believed, along with quite a few prominent Greek women and men.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea, they went there themselves to incite and agitate the crowds.
The brothers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy remained in Berea.
Those who escorted Paul brought him to Athens and then returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.

units.label: Paul provoked in Athens
units.note: the city full of idols, the philosophers curious

verses.text: While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day.

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also began to debate with him. Some of them asked, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign gods.” They said this because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
So they took Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, where they asked him, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears, and we want to know what they mean.”
Now all the Athenians and foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.

units.label: Paul's address at the Areopagus
units.note: the unknown God now proclaimed, judgment and resurrection

verses.text: Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very {{deisidaimon|religious}}.

For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something {{agnostos|unknown}}, I now proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands.
Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands.
God intended that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.
‘For in Him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are His offspring.’
Therefore, being offspring of God, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.
Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to {{metanoeo|repent}}.
For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.”
When they heard about the {{anastasis|resurrection}} of the dead, some began to mock him, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.”
At that, Paul left the Areopagus.
But some joined him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.

deisidaimon.gloss: Religious, reverent toward the gods, a word that can carry the shade of superstitious. Paul opens with a careful compliment that is also a probe: the Athenians are scrupulously devout, yet their very altars betray that they do not know the God they worship. It is a bridge to the gospel, not flattery.

agnostos.gloss: Unknown, unknowable by human effort. The root lies behind the English agnostic. The Athenians hedged their piety with an altar to an unknown god; Paul seizes on it to announce that this God has now made Himself known in the Creator revealed and in the risen Man He appointed.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, to change one's mind and turn. It is more than regret; it is a turning of the whole person from idols to the living God. Paul says God now commands all people everywhere to repent, a universal summons grounded in the coming judgment and the resurrection of Christ.

anastasis.gloss: Resurrection, a rising again. It is the hinge of Paul's argument and the point at which the philosophers divide: God has given proof to all by raising the appointed Man from the dead. The resurrection guarantees the judgment and validates the claim that Jesus is Lord of every nation.

basic.context: Paul moves through three cities. In Thessalonica he reasons from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise, wins some, and is chased out by a jealous mob crying that he proclaims another king, Jesus. In Berea the hearers eagerly test his message against Scripture and many believe. In Athens, provoked by a city full of idols, Paul debates the philosophers and then addresses the Areopagus about the unknown God.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch how Paul adapts his approach without changing his message. With Jews and God-fearers he argues from Scripture; with pagan philosophers who do not accept the Scriptures he begins from creation, conscience, and even their own poets, then drives to the same points, repentance, judgment, and the resurrection of Jesus. The key question the passage raises is how far a Christian may engage pagan thought while still preaching Christ crucified and risen.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls the Athenians deisidaimon, very religious, a careful bridge. He points to their altar to an agnostos, unknown, god and announces the God now made known. He ends by commanding all to metanoeo, repent, because of the coming judgment proved by the anastasis, the resurrection, the very word that splits his audience.
basic.typology: The altar to an unknown god pictures the longing of the nations, groping after a God they cannot reach. Paul presents Christ, the appointed Man, as the true meeting point of God and humanity. The scattering of the nations from one man and the fixing of their boundaries recall Genesis, now gathered under the risen Lord.
basic.christ: In every city Christ is the message: the suffering and rising Messiah of the Scriptures at Thessalonica and Berea, and the appointed Man raised from the dead at Athens. His resurrection is the proof God gives to all that He will judge the world in righteousness through Him.
basic.god: God is the Creator who needs nothing and gives everything, Lord of heaven and earth, sovereign over the nations and their times and places. He is not distant but near, and He now commands all people everywhere to repent, no longer overlooking ignorance.
basic.crossReferences: The Thessalonian letters grow from this visit. Genesis 1 and Deuteronomy 32 stand behind Paul's account of creation and the nations. Isaiah 44 mocks the folly of idols, as Paul does at Athens. Romans 1 explains the ignorance and idolatry Paul confronts.
basic.oneStory: The gospel confronts the pagan mind at the intellectual capital of the world. The one story of Scripture, the Creator reclaiming the nations through His Son, reaches the philosophers of Athens, where the risen Christ is announced as Lord of every people and the ground of the coming judgment.

context.literary:
Luke gives this chapter a three part design, and each city is a different kind of test for the gospel. In Thessalonica the test is political, in Berea it is intellectual honesty before the Scriptures, and in Athens it is the clash with Greek wisdom. The chapter moves from synagogue to synagogue to marketplace and court, and the audience steadily widens from Jews and God-fearers to philosophers who have never heard Moses.

The first two scenes are paired by contrast. The same opening move, reasoning from the Scriptures, produces riot in Thessalonica and careful study in Berea. Luke does not hide the fact that the Thessalonians also believed, 17:4, but he gives the Bereans a title of honour. The pairing teaches by comparison what a good hearing of the word looks like.

The Athens section is the longest and has the clearest internal structure. It opens with Paul's reaction, verse 16, then with his daily routine, verse 17, and then with the philosophers' reaction, verses 18 to 21, which frames the speech. The speech itself, verses 22 to 31, runs in a deliberate order, from the altar, to God as creator and giver, to humanity's single origin and search, to the folly of images, and finally to the call to repent in view of judgment and resurrection. Luke's reader hears the climax in the last words, and the response in verses 32 to 34 splits into mockery, interest and faith.

Notice what the speech does not contain. There is no quotation of the Old Testament by name and the name of Jesus does not appear; He is 'the Man He has appointed.' Yet the allusions to Scripture run through almost every line, and the speech ends with exactly the facts, judgment and resurrection, that Luke's reader knows are the heart of the gospel.
context.historical:
Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a free city governed by its own officials. Luke calls them politarchs in 17:6, a rare title that inscriptions from the region have confirmed. The city lay on the Egnatian Way, which linked the Adriatic to the east, so news travelled quickly. Honours paid to the emperor were part of civic life, and that explains why the charge of verse 7 was dangerous: to say there was another king was to speak against Caesar. The bond collected from Jason in verse 9 was security that the troublemakers would depart.

Paul's own letters show that the work in Thessalonica lasted longer than three Sabbaths in the synagogue. He worked day and night so as not to burden them, 1 Thessalonians 2:9, and the church received help from Philippi more than once, Philippians 4:16. Many of its members were Gentiles who had turned from idols, 1 Thessalonians 1:9.

Berea was a smaller town off the main road, and the Jews there were more open.

Athens in the middle of the first century was no longer a political power, but it was the intellectual capital of the Greek world, with its temples, statues, schools and heritage. Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and that death was simply the end. Stoics taught a pervading divine reason and a self-sufficient life. Both are present in Paul's audience. 'Babbler' in verse 18 renders a word that pictures a bird pecking at seeds, hence someone who picks up scraps of ideas.

The Areopagus is named for the hill of Ares, and the term also describes the council that met there. Whether Paul stood on the hill or before the council in another place is disputed, but the setting is clearly one of formal inquiry. Ancient writers report altars to unknown gods in Athens, which gives Paul his opening. Aeschylus's play on the founding of this court has Apollo say that there is no resurrection of the dead, a line that Athenians would know, which helps explain the mockery in verse 32.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on a large range of earlier Scripture without naming it, and it sets patterns that the rest of the New Testament follows.

The Thessalonian preaching rests on the claim that the Christ must suffer and rise, 17:3, which is Jesus' own reading of the Old Testament in Luke 24:25-27 and 24:44-47, and Peter's reading of Psalm 16 at Pentecost, Acts 2:25-31. In the Thessalonian letters Paul sums up the result of this preaching: they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, 1 Thessalonians 1:9-10. It is almost the Areopagus speech in a sentence.

The speech itself is thick with the Old Testament. The Creator who needs nothing, verses 24 to 25, recalls Isaiah 42:5 and Psalm 50:9-12. The God who does not dwell in temples recalls Solomon's own prayer, 1 Kings 8:27, and Isaiah 66:1-2, which Stephen quoted, Acts 7:48-50. The single origin of nations and their fixed boundaries recall Genesis 1:26-28 and Deuteronomy 32:8. The mockery of images is the same as in Isaiah 44:9-20 and Psalm 115:4-8. The coming judgment recalls Psalm 9:8 and 96:13. Paul used a shorter version of the argument at Lystra, Acts 14:15-17.

Later in the New Testament Paul develops the same line of thought in Romans 1:18-25, where humanity knows God yet exchanges His glory for images, and in 1 Corinthians 2:1-5, written shortly after Athens, where he says he came to Corinth determined to know nothing but Christ crucified. The Bereans' habit of examining the Scriptures daily becomes a pattern for the church, as Paul urges testing everything in 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wanted his readers to see how the gospel meets different audiences without bending. Paul adapts his starting point, the Scriptures for the synagogue and creation for the philosophers, but his destination never changes: the living God, the call to repent, a coming judgment and the risen Jesus. The Athens speech is Luke's model of how to speak to people with no biblical background, and it is meant to be studied.

He wanted to commend the Bereans' habit of testing what they hear against Scripture. The tribute is placed beside a story of mob violence so that readers compare how people respond to truth. He also wanted to show that opposition tends to follow the gospel from city to city and that its engine is often jealousy, 17:5, and that charges against the church are framed in political terms, as they had been against Jesus.

He wanted readers, particularly Gentile readers, to see that Christianity is not a foreign cult adding one more god to the Athenian shelf but the claim that the one God who made everything has now acted in history, 17:31. For readers who might feel that the resurrection is an embarrassing point to raise before sophisticated people, Luke shows Paul raising it anyway and shows that some believed. The result is that the church is free to speak without apology.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The speech at the Areopagus is described, not commanded. It gives an example of how the apostle spoke to a particular audience at a particular moment, and it does not require every believer to quote poets or to begin with an altar. What is meant to carry forward is the pattern: start where the hearers are, use what they know, and do not stop until the claim about Jesus and the resurrection has been made.

The quotations of Greek poets in verse 28 do not give approval to everything in those poets or to the religion they describe. Paul uses a line that points in the right direction, and then insists that God is not like gold or stone. Quoting a person's own sources is a bridge, not an endorsement.

The record of response is also descriptive. Some mocked, some wanted to hear more, and some believed. Luke does not say the sermon failed or succeeded. The only prescription in the passage is the one inside the speech: God commands all people everywhere to repent. The call is for hearers and for the church that speaks to them. And the Bereans are a straightforward example that the church is meant to follow: receiving the word eagerly and checking it daily against the Scriptures.

debates.question: Was the Areopagus speech a good model, or did Paul fail at Athens?

views.label: A model of contextual preaching
views.case: Paul begins with their religiosity and an altar they had built, quotes their poets, and still reaches the same points as in the synagogue. Luke records no rebuke of the speech and notes converts, including a member of the court itself, verse 34. Those who hold this view say that the speech shows a faithful method for engaging unbelievers.

views.label: A misstep Paul later regretted
views.case: Others read Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 2:1-5, written soon after, where he resolves to know nothing but Christ crucified, as a correction of an overly philosophical approach. They point to the small number of converts and note that Athens never appears as a thriving church in the letters.

views.label: A faithful message with a normal mixed response
views.case: A third view says the speech should not be judged by numbers. The pattern of mockery, curiosity and faith is exactly what Luke shows elsewhere, such as at Pentecost, Acts 2:12-13, and the message in verse 31 is the cross's sequel, the resurrection.

debates.bearing: The text itself shows that Paul did not water down the resurrection and judgment, which are the offence of the gospel, and he held to the one truth throughout. Whatever lessons Paul drew for Corinth, the Athenian speech contains the core of the gospel that his later letters defend.

debates.question: What does Paul's use of Greek poets say about general revelation?

views.label: A real, though partial, knowledge of God
views.case: Paul says God intended that people would seek Him and that He is not far from each one of us, verses 27 and 28. The poets' lines reflect something true, and Romans 1:19-20 and 2:14-15 teach that all people have some knowledge of God and conscience.

views.label: Knowledge that humanity suppresses
views.case: Others stress that Paul calls the Athenian worship ignorance, verse 30, and speaks of groping, verse 27. Romans 1:18-25 says people suppress the truth and exchange the glory of God for images. On this view the poets' lines are borrowed but not understood.

debates.bearing: Both views fit the speech. Paul affirms that God is near and knowable, and he also declares that humanity has gone wrong and needs to repent. Revelation in creation leaves people without excuse; only the gospel gives them the way home.

debates.question: Where did Paul speak, and what kind of setting was it?

views.label: Before the council of the Areopagus
views.case: The word describes the body of men who met there, and the question in verse 19 and the presence of a member of the council in verse 34 suggest a formal hearing about a new teaching.

views.label: On the hill of Ares in open air
views.case: Others take it as the hill itself, a place where people were accustomed to gather. The phrase 'in the midst of' in verse 22 fits an open space.

debates.bearing: The difference does not change the message, though it reminds readers that Paul was in a place of cultural authority.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is how Paul's reaction in verse 16 is described. He was 'deeply disturbed,' from paroxyno, the same root as the paroxysmos of the quarrel with Barnabas in the previous study. It means to be stirred up, provoked, and Luke uses the verb in the passive, as though the sight of the city had acted on him. The provocation produces action, for the next verse says he reasoned daily. It is the same energy as Paul's anger, turned toward speech.

The verb for what Paul does in the synagogue, 17:2 and 17:17, is dialegomai, 'reasoned,' the verb the Corinth chapter will also use. In 17:3 he is said to be explaining, dianoigo, the verb Luke uses for the Lord opening Lydia's heart, and proving, paratithemi, a verb that means to lay beside, as one lays evidence on a table. Paul opens the Scriptures and sets the evidence out. The Christ 'had to' suffer, dei, a word of divine necessity that runs through Luke's Gospel, as in Luke 24:26.

The Thessalonians' charge in verse 6 says Paul and Silas 'turned the world upside down,' from anastatoo, to stir up, to cause an uproar. The word is exaggeration, and Luke may intend a gentle irony, since the charge says more than the accusers intend about what the gospel does.

The Bereans are 'more noble-minded,' eugenes in the comparative, which literally means better born and came to mean having the qualities of nobility, and they 'examined' the Scriptures, anakrino, a verb from legal inquiry that means to sift evidence. They did this daily. The eagerness, prothumia, is a readiness of mind.

In Athens the philosophers call Paul a spermologos, a seed-picker, in verse 18. The Athenian curiosity is described in verse 21, where Luke says the whole city had time for nothing but hearing and passing on the latest idea. Paul answers that the God he proclaims is not far away, and the word in verse 27 for how people might 'reach out' for Him is psēlaphao, to feel about, grope, as a blind man might in the dark. The same verb describes the disciples touching the risen Jesus in Luke 24:39. The Greeks' seeking is groping; the risen One can be touched.

God 'overlooked' the times of ignorance, in verse 30, from huperorao, which literally means to look over or past, as one overlooks an offence without punishing it for the time. Romans 3:25 speaks of God passing over former sins, and Acts 14:16 speaks of God allowing the nations to go their own way. The overlooking is patience, not approval, and it ends with the command to repent.

Finally, in verse 31 God has given 'proof,' pistis, to all by raising the Man from the dead. The word that elsewhere means faith here means the ground of faith, the assurance on which a person may believe.

typology.type: Another king, Jesus, and the charge against Christ
typology.fulfillment: The accusers in Thessalonica say that these men defy Caesar's decrees by proclaiming another king, verse 7. The charge repeats the one brought against Jesus before Pilate, the charge that He said He was Christ, a King, Luke 23:2, and the priests' cry that they had no king but Caesar, John 19:15. The correspondence is that the servants are treated like their Master, John 15:20. The escalation is that the kingdom the charge fears is real: Jesus is King of kings, Revelation 19:16. It falls short only in that Paul's accusers misunderstand the kind of kingdom it is, one that does not overthrow Rome by the sword, John 18:36.

Solomon confessed that heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain God, much less a house, 1 Kings 8:27. Paul says the same at Athens, verse 24. The temple pointed to God's dwelling among His people, and in Christ that dwelling takes a person: Jesus spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21. Believers together become a house for God by the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short in that a building could not travel or embrace the nations, whereas the risen Christ is present wherever His people gather, Matthew 18:20.

Paul says that God made every nation from one man, verse 26, recalling Adam as the head of the whole race. Paul sets Adam beside Christ, who is the man appointed to judge, verse 31. In Romans 5:12-19 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and 15:45 he calls Adam the pattern of the one to come and Christ the last Adam. The correspondence is that one man's act affects all. The escalation is that Christ brings life where Adam brought death. The type falls short in that Adam could not save his descendants, which is why the new Man had to come.

The Bereans' daily search of the Scriptures to see whether Paul's teaching was true matches the instruction for Israel's king to read the law all his life, Deuteronomy 17:18-19, and the blessing on the one who meditates on the law day and night, Psalm 1:2. In Christ, the Scriptures are read as testifying of Him, John 5:39. The pattern falls short only if the searching stops short of the person; the Bereans move on from checking to believing, verse 12.

study.christ:
Christ is announced in this chapter in three different registers, and each one fits its audience.

In the synagogue Paul's method is to show from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise. The claim that the Messiah must suffer was not the Jewish expectation, and Paul does not weaken it. He does as Jesus did on the road to Emmaus, opening the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms to show that the Messiah must suffer and enter into glory, Luke 24:25-27. Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 are among the texts such reasoning would cover, and Psalm 16:10, which Peter and Paul both read as pointing to the resurrection, Acts 2:27 and 13:35. The statement 'This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ' ties the Messiah of Scripture to a particular man.

In the marketplace Christ is the king the Thessalonian mob accuses the apostles of proclaiming. The charge is wrong about the politics but right about the title. Jesus is Lord of all, Acts 10:36, and no decree of Caesar overrules Him. The cost of this confession falls on believers, as 1 Thessalonians 2:14 says.

At the Areopagus Christ is the Man God has appointed to judge the world with justice, verse 31. The phrase draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives authority, and on Jesus' own claim that the Father has given Him authority to judge because He is the Son of Man, John 5:27. The proof is the resurrection, which marks Him out as God's chosen. The one hidden behind the altar to an unknown God is made known in the risen Jesus, and John 1:18 says that the Son has made the Father known.

The passage also sets the scope of Christ's work: all people everywhere are commanded to repent, and a day is fixed. Christ is not only a personal saviour but the one before whom the whole world will stand.

A caution: the altar itself is not a hidden prophecy of Christ. Paul uses it as a point of contact and does not say the Athenians were secretly worshipping Him. What the passage shows is that the Christ of the Scriptures is also the answer to the questions the nations ask.
study.god:
The Areopagus speech is one of the fullest accounts of who God is in the book of Acts, and it is built as a deliberate contrast with the gods of Athens.

God is the maker. He made the world and everything in it, verse 24. No Greek school could claim this of its gods, which were part of the world rather than its source. He is Lord of heaven and earth by right of making.

He is self-sufficient. He is not served by human hands as though He needed anything, verse 25. All religion that treats God as a hungry patron is exposed. Every offering is a gift returned to the giver, as Psalm 50:9-12 says.

He is the giver of life and breath and everything else. People do not rise from their bed or take their next breath except by His gift. This turns worship from a bargain into thanks.

He is sovereign over history. He set the times and boundaries of nations, verse 26. Empires rise and fall within the limits He sets, and the purpose was that people should seek Him. His rule has a goal, which is that humanity should find Him.

He is near. In the same breath that Paul speaks of God's greatness, he declares that He is not far from each one of us. The transcendent God is also the God who sustains every life, and verse 28 says that in Him we live and move and have our being. The doctrine of God must hold both the otherness and the nearness.

He is patient, then insistent. He overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, which is mercy, and He now commands repentance, which is the end of that stage. God's patience is not indifference.

He is judge. He has set a day. The same God who gives breath will judge the world with justice, and He has given proof by raising a Man from the dead. Judgment is not a threat added to the gospel but part of what it means to say that God is just.

For worship, the passage means that images and temples cannot hold or please Him. It also means that praise is the right response of a creature who has received everything.

crossReferences.note: Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples that the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. Paul's reasoning in the synagogue in Acts 17:2-3 is this same method, a reading of the whole Old Testament as pointing to a suffering and risen Messiah.

The charge brought against Jesus before Pilate was that He claimed to be Christ, a King, and forbade payment of taxes to Caesar. The accusation against Jason and the missionaries in Acts 17:7 is its echo, and shows that the servants face the same kind of charge as the Lord.

Paul's own summary of what the Thessalonians had done: turned from idols to serve the living and true God and to wait for His Son from heaven. It confirms that the preaching in Thessalonica reached Gentiles and that the shape of the message was the same as at Athens.

The psalm of David that Peter and Paul both read as pointing to the resurrection of the Christ, Acts 2:25-31 and 13:35-37. It is among the texts Paul would have used in the synagogue when proving that the Christ must rise from the dead.

Paul tells the Thessalonians to test everything and hold on to what is good. The command fits the Berean habit of Acts 17:11, and shows that Paul valued the church's testing of his own words against Scripture.

At Lystra Paul gives a shorter form of the Athens argument to a pagan crowd. God is the living Creator, past generations were allowed to go their own ways, and yet He left a witness in the rain and crops. It shows that the Areopagus speech was no one-off but Paul's regular approach to pagan audiences.

A sharp satire on idol makers who burn half a log for warmth and carve the other half into a god. Paul's statement that the divine is not like gold or silver or stone, verse 29, draws on this tradition of Israel's ridicule of images.

When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, He set their boundaries. The idea stands behind Paul's remark that God determined the appointed times and the boundaries of the lands, verse 26, and shows that the nations' history was never outside His hand.

Paul's fuller argument that God's invisible qualities have been clearly seen since creation and that people exchanged His glory for images. It is the theology behind the Areopagus speech's claim that people ought to have known the Creator and should not worship images.

Soon after Athens Paul tells Corinth that he came in weakness and resolved to know nothing but Jesus Christ and Him crucified. Whatever it says about his approach at Athens, it shows that his message always had the cross at the centre.

One like a son of man receives authority, glory and a kingdom, and all peoples serve him. The 'Man He has appointed' to judge the world in Acts 17:31 stands in this tradition, and Jesus claimed the title in John 5:27.

study.oneStory:
The Athens speech tells the whole Bible's story in one breath, aimed at people who have never heard it. Creation: the God who made the world and gives life and breath. Humanity: one man, one family, set in times and places so that they might seek Him, which is Genesis 1 and 2 retold. Fall: the nations have turned to images and ignorance, as Romans 1 describes. Redemption: God now commands repentance and has appointed a Man to judge, proved by the resurrection. New creation: the day He has fixed. Paul is giving Athens the story from the beginning, because they had no Old Testament to start from.

The chapter also answers a question left from the tower of Babel, Genesis 11. There the nations were scattered and their boundaries fixed, yet the Bible's promise to Abraham was that all nations would be blessed. Paul says the scattering was itself part of a plan that they should seek God, and the gospel is the moment when the plan is revealed. The Thessalonian church, the Berean readers and the Athenian believers are first fruits of that gathering.

It also continues the thread of God's attitude to the nations' ignorance. Psalm 98 and Psalm 9 speak of Him judging the world in righteousness; Isaiah 49:6 speaks of a light to the nations. Luke 24:47 says repentance and forgiveness would be preached to all nations beginning at Jerusalem, and Acts 17 shows that preaching reaching the heart of Greek culture.

The story ends in the day Paul speaks of. Every knee will bow, Philippians 2:10-11, and a great multitude from every nation will stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9. Revelation 21 shows the nations walking by the light of the city, and no idol remains. The Athenian altar to an unknown God and the pantheon around it give way to a city whose temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, Revelation 21:22. The Bereans' daily reading and the apostle's reasoning together keep the story open until that day.

quiz.q: What made the Bereans more noble-minded than the Thessalonians?

options.text: They received the message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to test it.
options.note: Luke praises their eager reception joined to careful testing of the message against Scripture.

options.text: They believed Paul immediately without any hesitation.
options.note: Many did believe, but their nobility lay in eager yet testing hearing, not in uncritical acceptance.

options.text: They were more educated than the people of Thessalonica.
options.note: The text commends their attitude to Scripture, not their level of education.

options.text: They rejected the Scriptures in favour of Paul's authority.
options.note: The opposite is true: they weighed Paul's message by the Scriptures.

quiz.q: How did Paul begin his address to the Athenian philosophers?

options.text: From their altar to an unknown god and from the one Creator of all.
options.note: Paul starts with the altar and creation, common ground the pagans could grant, then moves to the gospel.

options.text: By quoting the Hebrew prophets to prove Jesus is the Messiah.
options.note: That was his method in the synagogue; with pagans who did not accept Scripture he began from creation and their own poets.

options.text: By condemning the city and refusing any common ground.
options.note: He was provoked by the idols, yet he engaged them, beginning with their altar rather than pure condemnation.

options.text: By affirming that all their gods were valid paths to truth.
options.note: Paul denied their idols; he did not endorse them.

quiz.q: On what basis does Paul say God now commands everyone to repent?

options.text: Because God has set a day of judgment, proven by raising the appointed Man from the dead.
options.note: Paul grounds the call to repent in the coming judgment guaranteed by the resurrection of Jesus.

options.text: Because idolatry is foolish and beneath rational people.
options.note: He does expose the folly of idols, but the stated ground for repentance is the judgment secured by the resurrection.

options.text: Because the Athenians were more religious than most.
options.note: He notes their religiosity as a bridge, not as the reason to repent.

options.text: Because God will overlook their ignorance forever.
options.note: Paul says God once overlooked ignorance but now commands repentance; He will not overlook it forever.

quiz.q: Why did the mob in Thessalonica accuse Paul of defying Caesar?

options.text: Because he proclaimed another king, Jesus, which sounded like treason.
options.note: The charge was that Paul preached another king, Jesus, against Caesar's decrees.

options.text: Because he had led a violent revolt in the city.
options.note: There was an uproar, but it was stirred by his opponents; the accusation centred on proclaiming Jesus as king, not on a revolt he led.

options.text: Because he refused to pay Roman taxes.
options.note: Taxes are not in view; the charge concerned proclaiming another king.

options.text: Because he denied that God exists.
options.note: Paul proclaimed the living God and the risen Christ, not atheism.

quiz.q: How did the Athenians respond to Paul's message about the resurrection?

options.text: Some mocked, some wanted to hear more, and some believed.
options.note: Luke records all three responses, including the conversion of Dionysius and Damaris.

options.text: The whole council was persuaded and believed at once.
options.note: Some did believe, but many mocked or deferred; it was not a wholesale conversion.

options.text: They arrested Paul and put him on trial for his life.
options.note: They debated and dismissed him, but there was no trial for his life here.

options.text: They all rejected him and no one believed.
options.note: Some did believe, including Dionysius the Areopagite and Damaris.

questions: The Bereans received the word eagerly yet tested everything by Scripture. How well do you hold together an open heart and a discerning mind when you hear teaching?
Paul was deeply disturbed by a city full of idols. What are the idols of your own culture, and does their grip on people move you as they moved Paul?
Paul honoured what truth the Athenians held while still calling them to repent. Where do you find it hardest to combine respect for others with faithfulness to the whole gospel?
Paul says God is not far from each one of us and commands all to repent. Is there an area where God is near and calling you to turn to Him afresh?
The resurrection was the point where Paul's hearers divided. How does the reality of the risen, appointed Judge shape the way you live and speak this week?

translationNotes.note: Very religious renders a Greek word that can also carry the sense of superstitious. Paul's opening is a careful, double-edged compliment, acknowledging their devotion while exposing its ignorance. Footnote markers in the source were omitted when building the verse text.
From one man renders literally from one; some manuscripts read from one blood. The sense is the same, that God made every nation from a single origin, underscoring the unity of the human race.

Paul cites pagan writers: for in Him we live and move and have our being is likely from Epimenides, and we are His offspring from the poem Phainomena by Aratus. Paul uses their words to press home the Creator's claim.
